Finding label errors with labelnoise

Source: vignettes/labelnoise.Rmd
labelnoise.Rmd

Labels in real data are often wrong: a coder picks the neighbouring category, a respondent’s answer is ambiguous, a form is keyed in badly. Wrong labels in training data cost accuracy; wrong labels in test data make the reported accuracy meaningless.

labelnoise finds examples whose given label is probably wrong. It needs only two things:

  1. the given labels, and
  2. out-of-sample predicted class probabilities from any classifier, for example from cross-validation.

It then applies confident learning (Northcutt, Jiang and Chuang, 2021): per-class confidence thresholds decide which examples confidently belong to another class than their label, and the counts are used to estimate how many labels are wrong and which ones.

library(labelnoise)

A first look with simulated data

simulate_label_noise() creates a dataset where we know which labels are wrong. It returns predictions in the yardstick convention: a label column and one .pred_<class> column per class.

sim <- simulate_label_noise(n = 1000, noise_rate = 0.1, signal = 3, seed = 1)
sim
#> # A tibble: 1,000 × 6
#>    true  given .pred_A .pred_B .pred_C .pred_D
#>    <fct> <fct>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
#>  1 A     A     0.813    0.116  0.0338  0.0381 
#>  2 A     A     0.924    0.0235 0.0146  0.0376 
#>  3 B     B     0.0300   0.876  0.0180  0.0759 
#>  4 D     D     0.00662  0.0108 0.0194  0.963  
#>  5 A     A     0.713    0.142  0.0844  0.0603 
#>  6 C     B     0.0186   0.0481 0.929   0.00397
#>  7 D     D     0.0132   0.0263 0.00723 0.953  
#>  8 B     B     0.159    0.762  0.00888 0.0701 
#>  9 B     B     0.0161   0.928  0.0251  0.0312 
#> 10 A     A     0.846    0.0200 0.0186  0.115  
#> # ℹ 990 more rows

find_label_issues() returns one row per example:

issues <- find_label_issues(sim, truth = given)
issues
#> # A tibble: 1,000 × 5
#>     .row given predicted label_quality is_label_issue
#>    <int> <fct> <fct>             <dbl> <lgl>         
#>  1     1 A     A                0.813  FALSE         
#>  2     2 A     A                0.924  FALSE         
#>  3     3 B     B                0.876  FALSE         
#>  4     4 D     D                0.963  FALSE         
#>  5     5 A     A                0.713  FALSE         
#>  6     6 B     C                0.0481 TRUE          
#>  7     7 D     D                0.953  FALSE         
#>  8     8 B     B                0.762  FALSE         
#>  9     9 B     B                0.928  FALSE         
#> 10    10 A     A                0.846  FALSE         
#> # ℹ 990 more rows

Sort the flagged examples by label_quality to review the most suspicious ones first:

flagged <- issues[issues$is_label_issue, ]
head(flagged[order(flagged$label_quality), ])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>    .row given predicted label_quality is_label_issue
#>   <int> <fct> <fct>             <dbl> <lgl>         
#> 1   638 C     A               0.00189 TRUE          
#> 2   385 D     A               0.00328 TRUE          
#> 3   509 D     C               0.00392 TRUE          
#> 4    51 A     B               0.00463 TRUE          
#> 5   846 C     B               0.00493 TRUE          
#> 6   482 B     A               0.00503 TRUE

Because this is a simulation, we can check the result:

table(flagged = issues$is_label_issue, mislabelled = sim$given != sim$true)
#>        mislabelled
#> flagged FALSE TRUE
#>   FALSE   879   14
#>   TRUE      7  100

With tidymodels

In practice the probabilities come from resampling a model. Fit it with tune::fit_resamples() and save the predictions; labelnoise reads them directly and puts every example back in its original row.

We add a few errors to iris to see whether they are found.

library(parsnip)
library(workflows)

iris_noisy <- iris
flipped <- c(5, 30, 60, 80, 110, 140)
iris_noisy$Species[flipped] <- c(
  "versicolor", "virginica", "setosa", "virginica", "setosa", "versicolor"
)

wf <- workflow(Species ~ ., multinom_reg() |> set_engine("nnet"))
set.seed(1)
folds <- rsample::vfold_cv(iris_noisy, v = 5)
res <- tune::fit_resamples(
  wf, folds,
  control = tune::control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)
)

issues <- find_label_issues(res)
which(issues$is_label_issue)
#> [1]   5  30  60  80 110 134 140

The flagged row numbers refer to rows of iris_noisy, so you can join them back to the data for review. If you tuned several models with tune::tune_grid(), choose one with parameters = tune::select_best(...).

Any data frame of predictions works too, for example the output of tune::collect_predictions() or augment(): name the label column in truth, and the .pred_* columns are found automatically.

Is the dataset healthy?

health_summary() gives the overall picture: how many labels look wrong, which classes are affected most, and which pairs of classes get confused. Confused pairs often point to an unclear definition or coding guideline rather than to individual mistakes.

health_summary(sim, truth = given)
#> Label health
#> • Overall score: 0.915
#> • Estimated label issues: 85 of 1000 examples
#> 
#> Classes with the lowest label quality:
#> # A tibble: 4 × 7
#>   class     n num_label_issues label_issue_rate label_noise inverse_label_noise
#>   <fct> <int>            <int>            <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
#> 1 D       125               19           0.152       0.173               0.194 
#> 2 C       207               28           0.135       0.130               0.169 
#> 3 B       280               22           0.0786      0.116               0.103 
#> 4 A       388               16           0.0412      0.0800              0.0602
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: label_quality <dbl>

The underlying estimates are available separately: confident_joint(), estimate_joint(), noise_matrices() and num_label_issues().

Choosing a rule

find_label_issues() implements the five rank-and-prune rules of the paper through filter_by. The default, "prune_by_noise_rate", flags in each cell of the estimated joint distribution the examples with the largest margin towards the other class. In our simulations its accuracy was close to that of "both" and "prune_by_class"; "predicted_neq_given" is a simple baseline that flags every disagreement with the model. Use frac_noise below 1 to flag fewer, more certain examples.

Other modelling frameworks

The same functions accept

  • a label vector plus a probability matrix: find_label_issues(labels, pred_probs = probs);
  • an mlr3 ResampleResult or PredictionClassif from a learner with predict_type = "prob";
  • a caret train object fitted with trainControl(classProbs = TRUE, savePredictions = "final").

Repeated cross-validation is fine: predictions of the same example are averaged. Bootstrap resampling is not, because some rows never get an out-of-sample prediction.

Without any framework, cross-validation takes a few lines:

set.seed(1)
fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(iris)))
probs <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow(iris), 3, dimnames = list(NULL, levels(iris$Species)))
for (k in 1:5) {
  fit <- nnet::multinom(Species ~ ., data = iris[fold != k, ], trace = FALSE)
  probs[fold == k, ] <- predict(fit, iris[fold == k, ], type = "probs")
}
num_label_issues(iris$Species, pred_probs = probs)
#> [1] 4

Text classification: coding open answers

A common use is checking coded open-ended answers, such as industry or occupation codes assigned to free-text descriptions. The sketch below uses textrecipes for TF-IDF features and a penalised multinomial model. It is not run when this vignette is built, because it needs extra packages and a dataset survey with a description text column and a code factor.

library(tidymodels)
library(textrecipes)

rec <- recipe(code ~ description, data = survey) |>
  step_tokenize(description) |>
  step_tokenfilter(description, max_tokens = 5000) |>
  step_tfidf(description)
wf <- workflow(rec, multinom_reg(penalty = 0.01) |> set_engine("glmnet"))

folds <- vfold_cv(survey, v = 5, strata = code)
res <- fit_resamples(wf, folds, control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE))

review <- survey |>
  bind_cols(find_label_issues(res) |> select(-given)) |>
  filter(is_label_issue) |>
  arrange(label_quality)

health_summary(res)$overlapping_classes

With many fine-grained codes, start at a coarser level of the classification, where every class has enough examples for stable thresholds, and move down once the coarse level is clean.

Caveats

  • Probabilities must be out-of-sample. A model that has seen a label will usually agree with it, hiding the error.
  • Results are only as good as the classifier. With a weak classifier, many correct labels are flagged and the number of errors is overestimated. In our simulations with a weak classifier and 5% wrong labels, the estimated number of errors was several times the true number. Check the model’s cross-validated accuracy first.
  • A flag is a reason to look, not a verdict. Ambiguous examples that fit several classes are flagged too. Use the output to prioritise manual review.
  • Confident learning assumes that the chance of a wrong label depends on the true class, not on the individual example. Real errors often depend on how ambiguous the example is, so treat the ranking as a strong heuristic.

Relation to cleanlab

labelnoise is an independent implementation from the published papers, not a port of the Python package cleanlab. Its test suite compares results with cleanlab 2.9.0 on simulated data: the confident joint, the five filtering rules, num_label_issues() and the self-confidence and normalised-margin scores agree exactly. The calibrated joint differs only by cleanlab’s rounding to whole counts, and the confidence-weighted entropy uses a different map to [0, 1] with the same ranking.

References

Northcutt, C., Jiang, L., & Chuang, I. (2021). Confident learning: Estimating uncertainty in dataset labels. Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, 70, 1373–1411. https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.1.12125

Kuan, J., & Mueller, J. (2022). Model-agnostic label quality scoring to detect real-world label errors. ICML DataPerf Workshop. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18168246
